title: Vortex Dynamics in Magic-Angle Twisted Graphene
authors: Marta Perego, Peter Koopmann, Clara Galante Agero, Alexandra Mestre Torà, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Vadim Geshkenbein, Gianni Blatter, Thomas Ihn, Klaus Ensslin
abstract: We use a gate-defined Josephson junction (JJ) device made from twisted-layer graphene for studying vortex dynamics in two dimensions. The JJ sensor signals the presence of individual vortices in the superconducting leads nearby the junction through shifts in the Fraunhofer interference pattern of the magnetic-field-dependent critical current $I_c(B)$ across the junction. Rapid vortex fluctuations manifest as telegraph-type noise in time traces of the junction voltage $V(t)$. Measurements of $I_c(B)$ and $V(t)$ are interpreted in terms of multi-vortex processes where fast vortex fluctuations in the leads are modulated by quasi-stationary vortices trapped in the leads. The different timescales associated with these processes allow for their disentangling and quantitative analysis. Tracking the temperature dependence of the vortex-dynamical rates between $T = 7$ mK and $T = 120$ mK, we find that the creep type vortex motion is thermally activated above $T \approx 100$ mK, while the saturation of rates below $T \approx 80$ mK is suggestive of a sharp transition to macroscopic quantum tunneling of vortices.
summary: The research uses a Josephson junction made from twisted graphene to study how magnetic vortices move within the superconductor. By measuring changes in critical current and analyzing voltage noise over varying temperatures, the authors distinguish between thermal creep motion and regimes dominated by macroscopic quantum tunneling of these vortices.
main_problem: The study investigates vortex dynamics within two dimensions using a Josephson junction (JJ) fabricated from magic-angle twisted graphene.
main_result: Vortex motion exhibits distinct temperature dependencies: thermally activated creep above 100 mK, transitioning to behavior suggestive of macroscopic quantum tunneling below 80 mK.
method: Measurements involve analyzing the magnetic-field-dependent critical current $I_c(B)$ for Fraunhofer pattern shifts and monitoring time traces of junction voltage $V(t)$ for telegraphic noise signatures.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a gate-defined Josephson junction made from magic-angle twisted graphene, which acts as a sensor for vortices penetrating the superconducting leads. The analysis models vortex dynamics using concepts like Pearl-vortices and free-energy barriers.
key_observables: $I_c(B)$ (Fraunhofer pattern shifts), voltage noise $V(t)$ (telegraph noise), vortex entry/exit rates ($\Gamma_{nv}, \Gamma_v$), and temperature dependence of these rates.
important_parameters: Temperature range ($7 	ext{ mK}$ to $120 	ext{ mK}$), junction width ($W=1.1 \mu	ext{m}$), and characteristic energy scales related to thermal activation vs. quantum tunneling.
main_assumptions: The analysis separates fast vortex fluctuations from quasi-stationary trapped vortices, and rate calculations require careful correction for finite detector bandwidth ($\Gamma_{	ext{det}}$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate device schematics, show vortex detection via jumps in the Fraunhofer pattern (Fig. 1(c)), and detail the temperature evolution of vortex rates and tunneling actions (Fig. 6).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the experimental setup and observing basic vortex signatures in $I_c(B)$ to analyzing time-domain noise ($V(t)$) for rate extraction, culminating in a detailed analysis of temperature dependence across quantum tunneling and thermal regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly probes non-equilibrium dynamics (vortex motion) in superconducting mesoscopic systems using advanced graphene heterostructures, providing insights into quantum dissipation mechanisms relevant to superconducting electronics.
